data_disclaimer: General agronomic guidance compiled from public sugarcane extension literature. This file deliberately contains NO pesticide product names and NO chemical dosages. Chemical control decisions must come from your local agricultural extension officer, State Agricultural University or sugar factory cane department, based on an in-field inspection. Edit this file to match your local advisory.
safety_notice: AI-based result. Please verify important disease or chemical treatment decisions with a qualified agricultural expert.

healthy.label: Healthy Sugarcane
healthy.short_description: No clear visual disease symptoms were detected in the uploaded image.
symptoms: Uniform green leaf colour without large lesions
No red or brown internal discoloration visible
No powdery spore masses or whip-like structures visible
causes: Not applicable - the visible tissue appears normal in this image
immediate_actions: Continue routine field scouting at least once a week
Keep following your normal irrigation and nutrition schedule
Photograph and log the crop periodically so changes are easy to spot
management: Maintain field sanitation and remove crop debris between seasons
Keep drainage channels clear so water does not stagnate
Use certified, disease-free seed cane for the next planting
prevention: Practise crop rotation where possible
Avoid moving soil, tools or setts from an infected block into a clean block
Disinfect cutting tools between blocks

details: Follow the irrigation schedule generated by the irrigation module
Avoid prolonged waterlogging, which stresses roots even in a healthy crop

nutrient_advice: Continue the planned split fertilizer schedule
Base quantities on a laboratory soil test wherever possible
monitoring: Inspect the field again within 7 days
Upload another image in 7 to 14 days to build a health trend

red_rot.label: Red Rot
red_rot.short_description: Red rot is one of the most serious fungal diseases of sugarcane. It is associated with Colletotrichum falcatum and can cause rapid loss of an affected crop.
symptoms: Drying and yellowing of the third or fourth leaf from the top while lower leaves may still look green
Reddening of the internal stalk tissue, often with white or cream cross bands
A sour, alcoholic smell when an affected cane is split open
Hollow or shrunken internodes in advanced cases
causes: Infected or untreated seed cane (setts)
Carry-over of the pathogen in crop residue and soil
Wounds caused by borers or mechanical damage that create entry points
Prolonged waterlogging and poor drainage
Continuous cropping of a susceptible variety in the same field
immediate_actions: Isolate the affected area and avoid moving setts, soil or tools out of it
Uproot and safely dispose of severely affected clumps together with their stubble, following local guidance
Do not use cane from an affected block as seed material
Improve drainage so water does not stand in the affected patch
Report the outbreak to your local agricultural officer or factory cane department
management: Stop irrigation water from flowing from an infected block into a healthy block
Follow only locally approved fungicide or sett-treatment guidance issued by your extension service
Where the local advisory recommends it, plan a rotation with a non-host crop before replanting
Replant with a variety that has a good current local reaction to red rot
prevention: Always plant certified, disease-free seed cane
Follow locally recommended seed treatment before planting
Maintain field sanitation and destroy infected residue
Control stalk borers, which create infection wounds
Avoid continuous monoculture of a susceptible variety

irrigation_advice.summary: Reduce standing water. Waterlogging strongly favours red rot spread.
details: Avoid flood irrigation across an affected patch - it carries spores downstream
Improve drainage channels before the next irrigation
Prefer lighter, more frequent irrigation over heavy flooding in the affected area
If drip or furrow irrigation is available, use it to isolate blocks

nutrient_advice: Avoid a heavy single nitrogen dose on an affected crop - lush soft growth is more vulnerable
Potassium supports general plant vigour - follow soil-test-based local recommendations
Add well-decomposed organic matter to improve soil structure and drainage
Do not attempt to compensate for disease damage with extra fertilizer
monitoring: Inspect the affected block and its neighbours every 2 to 3 days
Split a few suspect canes lengthwise to check for internal reddening
Mark affected clumps so spread can be measured
Upload a follow-up image in 5 to 7 days to compare

severity_guidance.mild: A few isolated clumps affected. Remove them, improve drainage and monitor every 3 days.
severity_guidance.moderate: Several clumps across the block. Isolate the block, stop cross-block irrigation and contact your agricultural officer.
severity_guidance.severe: Widespread drying and internal reddening. Treat the block as a source of infection, plan safe disposal of residue and get an on-site expert inspection before replanting.

rust.label: Rust
rust.short_description: Sugarcane rust is a foliar fungal disease that reduces the photosynthetic area of the leaf and therefore reduces cane growth.
symptoms: Small elongated yellowish spots on the leaf that later turn orange-brown to reddish-brown
Raised pustules mainly on the lower leaf surface that release powdery spores
Pustules running parallel to the leaf veins
In heavy infection, leaves dry from the tip downwards
causes: Warm humid weather with long leaf wetness periods
Dense planting and poor air movement in the canopy
Susceptible variety grown continuously
Wind-borne spores from a neighbouring infected field
immediate_actions: Assess how much of the leaf area is covered before deciding on any action
Remove and safely dispose of heavily infected lower leaves where practical
Avoid overhead irrigation in the evening, which extends leaf wetness
Improve air movement by removing excess trash from the canopy
management: Follow locally approved fungicide guidance only if your extension officer confirms it is economically justified
Maintain balanced nutrition - a nitrogen-heavy crop is usually more susceptible
Plan the next crop with a variety showing a better local rust reaction
prevention: Maintain the recommended row spacing for your variety
Use healthy seed material
Detrash lower leaves at the locally recommended stage
Avoid excessive nitrogen

irrigation_advice.summary: Reduce leaf wetness duration. Avoid evening overhead irrigation.
details: Irrigate in the early morning so leaves dry during the day
Prefer furrow or drip irrigation over overhead sprinklers in an affected block
Do not let humidity build up under a dense canopy

nutrient_advice: Avoid excess nitrogen, which encourages soft susceptible growth
Maintain adequate potassium as part of a balanced schedule
Follow soil-test-based local recommendations for quantities
monitoring: Check the middle whorl leaves every 5 to 7 days
Record roughly what percentage of the leaf area carries pustules
Upload a follow-up image in 7 days to see whether the spread is slowing

severity_guidance.mild: Scattered pustules on a few lower leaves. Cultural measures are usually enough. Monitor weekly.
severity_guidance.moderate: Pustules on many leaves including the middle whorl. Improve airflow, correct nitrogen excess and consult your extension officer.
severity_guidance.severe: Extensive drying of leaves and heavy pustule cover. Get an on-site assessment - yield loss is likely and a control decision is needed quickly.

smut.label: Smut
smut.short_description: Sugarcane smut is caused by Sporisorium scitamineum and is recognised by a long black whip-like structure emerging from the top of the shoot.
symptoms: A long black or grey whip-like structure emerging from the growing point
Thin grassy shoots with narrow erect leaves
Stunted cane with shortened internodes
A black powdery spore mass released from the whip
causes: Infected seed cane carrying the pathogen
Spores surviving in soil and crop residue
Ratoon crops carrying over infection from the plant crop
Dry and warm conditions that favour spore spread
immediate_actions: Carefully cover the whip with a cloth or bag BEFORE cutting, so spores are not scattered
Remove the whole affected clump including the underground stubble
Destroy the removed material away from the field, following local guidance
Do not take seed material from an affected field
management: Remove whips regularly and early, before they burst
Avoid ratooning a badly affected crop - plough it out and replant with clean seed
Follow locally recommended seed treatment practice for the next planting
Switch to a variety with a better local smut reaction
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed cane
Follow local hot water or approved sett-treatment guidance where recommended
Rogue out affected clumps as soon as whips appear
Do not ratoon fields with a high smut incidence

irrigation_advice.summary: Irrigation is not the main driver, but crop stress increases susceptibility.
details: Avoid prolonged moisture stress, which weakens the crop
Keep a steady schedule rather than long dry gaps followed by heavy flooding
Do not move irrigation water directly from an affected block into a clean block

nutrient_advice: Maintain balanced nutrition so the crop is not stressed
Add organic matter to improve soil health
Follow soil-test-based local recommendations for quantities
monitoring: Walk the field every 3 to 5 days during the tillering stage and look for emerging whips
Count affected clumps so incidence can be tracked over time
Upload a follow-up image in 7 days

severity_guidance.mild: Occasional whips. Bag and rogue them immediately and keep scouting every 3 days.
severity_guidance.moderate: Whips appearing across the block. Rogue aggressively and plan not to ratoon this crop.
severity_guidance.severe: High incidence with many grassy stunted shoots. Consider ploughing out and replanting with certified clean seed after expert advice.

mosaic.label: Mosaic Disease
mosaic.short_description: Sugarcane mosaic is a viral disease that produces a patchy light-and-dark green pattern on young leaves. There is no chemical cure for a virus - management is preventive.
symptoms: Irregular light green, yellowish and normal green patches on young leaves
The pattern is clearest on the youngest fully opened leaf held against the light
General stunting and thinner canes in a badly affected crop
Symptoms may fade in hot weather and reappear later
causes: Planting infected seed cane - the main route of spread
Transmission by aphids moving between plants
Contaminated cutting tools
Presence of infected grasses and volunteer cane around the field
immediate_actions: Mark and rogue out clearly affected clumps including the stubble
Do not take seed material from affected plants
Disinfect cutting knives between plants and between blocks
Remove nearby weed grasses that can host the virus
management: There is no chemical that cures a viral infection in the plant - focus on clean seed and vector management
Manage aphid populations following locally approved guidance
Source next season's seed from a certified disease-free nursery
Use tissue-culture or heat-treated seed where your local programme offers it
prevention: Always plant certified virus-free seed cane
Maintain a clean seed nursery separated from the commercial crop
Control weeds and volunteer cane around field boundaries
Disinfect tools regularly

irrigation_advice.summary: Irrigation does not spread mosaic, but a stressed crop shows worse symptoms.
details: Keep irrigation regular to reduce additional stress on an infected crop
Avoid both prolonged drought stress and waterlogging
Do not increase water in the hope of curing the symptoms - it will not help

nutrient_advice: Maintain balanced nutrition to support the remaining healthy crop
Do not over-apply nitrogen to mask stunting
Follow soil-test-based local recommendations for quantities
monitoring: Inspect the youngest fully opened leaves weekly, ideally against sunlight
Record the number of affected clumps to track spread
Upload a follow-up image in 7 to 10 days

severity_guidance.mild: Faint mottling on a few plants. Rogue them and plan clean seed for next season.
severity_guidance.moderate: Clear mottling across many plants with some stunting. Rogue, manage aphids and do not use this field for seed.
severity_guidance.severe: Widespread mottling with significant stunting. Plan a full replant with certified virus-free seed after expert advice.

leaf_scald.label: Leaf Scald
leaf_scald.short_description: Leaf scald is a bacterial disease associated with Xanthomonas albilineans. It is notable for a sharp white pencil-line streak on the leaf and for a latent phase where infected plants look healthy.
symptoms: A narrow sharply defined white or cream pencil-line streak running along the leaf
Leaf tips that look scalded, bleached or burnt
Sudden wilting of an apparently healthy stalk
Side shoots sprouting abnormally from the stalk
A latent phase in which infected plants show no visible symptom at all
causes: Infected seed cane, including symptomless latent carriers
Contaminated cutting knives and harvesting equipment
Water stress that triggers latent infections to express
Movement of infected planting material between fields
immediate_actions: Disinfect cutting tools between every plant when working in a suspect block
Rogue out clearly affected clumps including the stubble
Do not use cane from the affected block as seed material
Avoid harvesting a clean block with equipment used in the affected block
management: Focus on clean seed - chemical control of a bacterial disease in the field is not usually practical
Follow locally recommended hot water seed treatment where your programme provides it
Choose varieties with a better local leaf scald reaction for replanting
Keep detailed records of which blocks supplied seed material
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed cane
Maintain strict tool hygiene
Avoid moisture stress, which triggers symptom expression
Establish a separate clean seed nursery

irrigation_advice.summary: Avoid drought stress - it triggers latent leaf scald infections to become visible.
details: Keep irrigation intervals regular and avoid long dry gaps
Do not let the crop reach severe wilting point
Avoid waterlogging as well, since root stress has the same effect

nutrient_advice: Maintain balanced nutrition to reduce overall crop stress
Avoid heavy single doses of nitrogen
Follow soil-test-based local recommendations for quantities
monitoring: Inspect weekly, paying attention to any sudden wilting of individual stalks
Look specifically for the sharp white pencil-line streak
Upload a follow-up image in 7 days
Remember that a clean-looking plant may still be a latent carrier

severity_guidance.mild: A few streaked leaves. Rogue affected clumps, tighten tool hygiene and monitor weekly.
severity_guidance.moderate: Streaking plus some sudden wilting. Isolate the block for seed purposes and consult your extension officer.
severity_guidance.severe: Widespread wilting and dieback. Get an expert inspection - a full replant with certified seed may be required.

yellow_leaf.label: Yellow Leaf Disease
yellow_leaf.short_description: Yellow leaf disease is associated with Sugarcane yellow leaf virus. Its characteristic sign is yellowing of the midrib on the underside of the leaf, spreading into the blade.
symptoms: Yellowing of the midrib, usually seen first on the underside of the leaf
Yellowing spreading from the midrib into the leaf blade
Yellowing that starts on older leaves and moves upward
Drying of the leaf tip and margins in advanced cases
Shortened top internodes and a bunched top in severe cases
causes: Infected seed cane
Transmission by aphids, especially the sugarcane aphid
Repeated ratooning of an infected crop
Crop stress that makes symptoms more visible
immediate_actions: Confirm it is not simply a nitrogen deficiency or waterlogging symptom - check the midrib specifically
Rogue out clearly affected clumps where incidence is still low
Manage aphid colonies following locally approved guidance
Do not take seed material from an affected field
management: There is no chemical cure for the virus - manage the vector and use clean seed
Use tissue-culture or heat-treated seed where available through your local programme
Avoid ratooning a badly affected crop
Maintain balanced nutrition so that true deficiency symptoms are not confused with the disease
prevention: Plant certified virus-free seed cane
Maintain a separate clean seed nursery
Scout regularly for aphid colonies on the underside of leaves
Limit the number of ratoons taken from an affected field

irrigation_advice.summary: Keep moisture steady. Both drought and waterlogging make yellowing look worse.
details: Avoid long dry intervals followed by heavy flooding
Ensure drainage is adequate - waterlogged roots cause similar-looking yellowing
Do not over-irrigate in an attempt to correct the colour

nutrient_advice: Check for nitrogen deficiency separately - it also causes general yellowing but not midrib yellowing
Maintain a balanced split nutrient schedule
Add organic matter to improve root health
Follow soil-test-based local recommendations for quantities
monitoring: Turn leaves over and inspect the midrib weekly
Record how many clumps show midrib yellowing
Upload a follow-up image in 7 to 10 days

severity_guidance.mild: Slight midrib yellowing on a few older leaves. Rogue, manage aphids and monitor weekly.
severity_guidance.moderate: Clear yellowing across many plants. Do not use this field for seed and consult your extension officer.
severity_guidance.severe: Widespread yellowing with bunched tops and stunting. Plan replanting with certified virus-free seed after expert advice.

unknown.label: Unknown / Low Confidence
unknown.short_description: The model could not reach a confident conclusion for this image. This is an honest 'not sure' result, not a diagnosis.
symptoms: Image quality, lighting, focus or framing may be limiting the analysis
The visible symptom may not match any class the model was trained on
More than one condition may be present in the same image
causes: Blurred, dark, over-exposed or very distant photograph
Symptoms too early to be visually distinctive
A condition outside the configured class list, including nutrient deficiency, pest damage or physical injury
immediate_actions: Retake the photograph in daylight, filling the frame with the affected leaf or stalk
Take separate close-up photographs of the leaf, the midrib underside and a split stalk
Do not apply any chemical treatment based on an uncertain result
Show the affected plant to a local agricultural officer
management: Treat this as a prompt to inspect the field in person, not as a diagnosis
Check for non-disease causes such as water stress, nutrient deficiency or borer damage
Record the date and location so the situation can be tracked
prevention: Keep using certified seed cane and standard field sanitation
Photograph the crop regularly so early changes are easier to catch

irrigation_advice.summary: Keep to your normal schedule until the cause is identified.
details: Do not increase or cut irrigation drastically based on an uncertain result
Check the soil moisture by hand at root depth to rule out simple water stress

nutrient_advice: Do not apply corrective fertilizer until the cause is identified
A laboratory soil test is the fastest way to rule out a nutrient problem
monitoring: Re-inspect within 2 to 3 days
Upload a clearer image once conditions allow
Ask an agricultural officer to inspect if the symptom is spreading
